newsitem.title: SLOVAKIA: Slovak c.bank adds crown risk, investors unfazed.
newsitem.headline: Slovak c.bank adds crown risk, investors unfazed.

text.p: The Slovak central bank on Thursday outlined its monetary policy for 1997, including a widening of the band in which it fixes the crown's exchange rate each day to slow the inflow of speculative capital.

National Bank of Slovakia (NBS) Governor Vladimir Masar told a news conference that effective January 1, the NBS would widen the crown's fluctuation band against its mark/dollar basket midpoint to plus/minus seven percent from five percent.
"In our monetary programme for 1997 we decided to widen the fluctuation band for fixing the crown to bring more uncertainty for the inflow of short-term, speculative capital," he said.

Slovakia's economy has proved resilient despite a turbulent political scene, with gross domestic product (GDP) growing 7.0 percent, year-on-year, for the first three quarters, and annual inflation at just 5.4 percent in November.
The NBS has long been battling a burgeoning money supply, which has been fuelled in part by speculative funds flowing into the country.

Slovak officials say they welcome investment, but with interest rates on the interbank money market ranging between 12.4 percent and 14.2 percent, many have been parking money in banks instead of using funds to restructure the economy.
Masar warned investors looking to park speculative "hot money" in Slovakia for short periods that the band, unlike this year, will be used to its full extent.

"We will use the fluctuation band in its entire range more significantly than we did in 1996, according to the market situation," Masar said. He added that he expected the move would be sufficient to achieve the central bank's aims.
In July, the NBS widened the fixing band to five percent from three percent for similar reasons.
The NBS's key M2 money supply had grown by 19.0 percent September, down from 22.1 percent in the same month of the previous year.

The NBS originally forecast M2 expansion of 11.6 percent, year-on-year, for 1996, but recently admitted it was more likely to be between 16-18 percent. Masar said the cental bank expects M2 growth to fall to 10.7 percent next year.
Market analysts said the wider band could have the desired effect, but they predicted it would not trigger large scale withdrawals of funds.

"The wider band may bring uncertanity, but I see it only as a psychological effect to keep out potential inflows of new hot money. More experienced investors here will probably not be frightened," Tibor Fratrik of ING Bank told Reuters.
Martin Hrozanyi, chief dealer at Slovenska Sporitelna, said he saw the move giving the NBS more room to eliminate the negative influence caused by a worsening trade balance.

"Now the NBS should have enough room to move the crown according to the development of the trade balance by, two or three percent for example, and prevent it from immediately reaching the fixing devaluation ceiling," Hrozanyi said.
He added that he did not expect higher than one percent move of the crown in the early next year.

Slovakia's foreign trade deficit widened to 42.52 billion crowns ($1.35 billion) for the first 10 months of 1996 from 37.17 billion crowns for the January-September period. The NBS on Thursday said it expected the trade balance to continue in this year trend at the beginning of 1997.
Meanwhile, rates may remain high next year as the central bank continues to battle inflation while trying to keep the economy from overheating.
Masar said the NBS is currently winning the war, but will have to push on its fight next year.
"We expect the favourable development of inflation to continue within the forecast range (of 4.9-5.8 percent)...but with a slower decrease in inflation than there has been so far."
($1=31.48 Slovak Crown)
